nama_domain: New Energy & Solar — utility-scale and rooftop solar PV (PLTS), the polysilicon-wafer-cell-module manufacturing chain, lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries, battery energy storage systems (BESS), and the wider 'new energy' industrial ecosystem, including its overcapacity/anti-involution cycle
kategori: Industry & Energy (industrial policy, energy transition, manufacturing overcapacity, critical minerals downstreaming, power sector reform)
tahun_mulai_china: Multiple waves. (1) 2004-2007: first export-led solar manufacturing boom, triggered by Germany's EEG feed-in tariff; Suntech Power listed on NYSE in December 2005 and its founder Shi Zhengrong briefly became China's richest man. (2) 2009-2013: domestic demand policies (Golden Sun programme, Building-Integrated PV subsidies, 2011 national feed-in tariff), followed by the FIRST overcapacity bust — Suntech and LDK Solar collapsed in 2013 under US anti-dumping duties (2012) and the EU trade probe. (3) 2013-2020: consolidation and cost-down; China became the world's largest installed solar market in 2015; LONGi's mono-wafer disruption from 2014 onward. (4) 2020-2023: the decisive phase — Xi Jinping's September 2020 '30-60' carbon pledge (peak CO2 by 2030, neutrality by 2060) turned solar + lithium batteries + EVs into the 'New Three' (新三样) export pillars, unleashing a capex wave that roughly quadrupled capacity in three years. (5) 2024-2026: the SECOND and much larger overcapacity bust plus the state-led 'anti-involution' (反内卷) correction, which was elevated to national policy on 1 July 2025 by the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission and written into the 15th Five-Year Plan. For Indonesia the operative reference wave is (4) and (5).
pemain_kunci_china: Polysilicon: Tongwei (通威), GCL Technology (协鑫), Daqo New Energy (大全), Xinte Energy (新特), East Hope (东方希望). Wafers/cells/modules: LONGi Green Energy (隆基绿能), JinkoSolar (晶科), Trina Solar (天合光能), JA Solar (晶澳), Canadian Solar (阿特斯), Tongwei Solar. Inverters and system integration: Huawei Digital Power and Sungrow (阳光电源) — ranked No.1 and No.2 globally in Wood Mackenzie's 2026 inverter ranking with near-identical scores of 93.9 and 93.7. Batteries: CATL (宁德时代), BYD FinDreams (弗迪电池), CALB (中创新航), EVE Energy (亿纬锂能), Gotion High-Tech (国轩高科), Sunwoda (欣旺达), REPT (瑞浦兰钧), Hithium (海辰储能). Energy storage integrators: 8 of the world's top 10 in 2025 were Chinese. State actors: NDRC, MIIT, National Energy Administration, State Administration for Market Regulation, the China Photovoltaic Industry Association (CPIA) as the cartel-adjacent coordinator, and Beijing Guanghe Qiancheng Technology (北京光和谦成) — the polysilicon capacity-retirement vehicle registered in December 2025. In Indonesia specifically the relevant Chinese actors are Trina Solar (Kendal SEZ), LONGi (Jakarta area), CATL/Brunp with Lygend Resources (Karawang and Halmahera), Tsingshan and Jiangsu Delong (nickel), plus Huayou Cobalt.
apa_yang_terjadi_di_china: China built a near-monopoly over the entire new-energy manufacturing chain, then drove it into the deepest loss-making cycle in its history, and is now using state power to force an orderly retreat. Mechanism: (a) Local governments competed to attract solar and battery gigafactories with free land, subsidised power, tax holidays and cheap state-bank credit, producing capacity decisions that were politically rather than commercially rational; (b) low barriers to entry in module assembly and LFP cell production plus a technology transition (PERC to TOPCon; NCM to LFP) invited a second wave of entrants who over-built the newest generation while incumbents' older lines were not yet written off; (c) the 2021-2023 export boom of the 'New Three' validated the capex, so capacity kept expanding into 2024 even as prices collapsed; (d) domestic demand policy then reversed — the June 2025 shift to market-based pricing for renewables (Document No. 136) removed the guaranteed tariff, causing a rush-to-install in H1 2025 and a demand cliff in 2026. The result: module prices below RMB 1/W, polysilicon below cash cost, sector-wide losses, mass layoffs, and dozens of bankruptcies. Beijing's response — 'anti-involution' (反内卷) — is a state-orchestrated supply-side reform: MIIT and NDRC summoned CEOs, banned below-cost bidding and selling, drafted mandatory energy-consumption standards to legally kill old lines, proposed a RMB 50 billion industry fund to buy and scrap roughly a third of polysilicon capacity, and legislated consumption taxes on PV cells and batteries to squeeze marginal producers out. Critically, an attempt at an explicit output-quota joint venture was halted by regulators on antitrust grounds, showing the limits of coordinated retrenchment. The overflow of this overcapacity is now the single most important external force shaping every other country's energy transition: solar modules and battery cells are being exported at prices no non-Chinese manufacturer can match, Chinese firms are relocating assembly to Southeast Asia to jump tariff walls, and importing countries are getting historically cheap clean energy hardware while their own manufacturing ambitions are being made unviable.
data_skala_china: MANUFACTURING SHARE (2024): polysilicon 93.2%, wafers 96.6%, cells 92.3%, modules 86.4% of world output. China's share of global solar patent applications reached ~65% by 2024, up from 13% in 2004. Chinese n-type TOPCon cells averaged 25.4% conversion efficiency in 2024 vs ~20% for US First Solar CdTe. PRICE COLLAPSE: module prices fell ~50% in 2023 and a further ~25% in 2024, dipping below RMB 1/watt; polysilicon fell from RMB 230,000/tonne to RMB 65,000/tonne during 2023 (-70%) and another ~40% in 2024. UTILISATION: global polysilicon output in 2025 was ~1.9 million tonnes against nameplate capacity above 3.2 million tonnes — utilisation below 60%. LOSSES: aggregate 2025 losses of listed Chinese solar companies estimated above RMB 50 billion (~US$7.3 billion). EMPLOYMENT: across 110 listed Chinese solar companies, headcount fell from 776,750 at the 2023 peak to 622,207 at end-2024 — a loss of 154,543 jobs in a single year, with more than 220,000 solar workers laid off or forced to change industries over the two-year downturn; the top five firms (LONGi, Tongwei, Trina, Jinko, JA Solar) cut workforce by over 30% in 2024, roughly 80,000-90,000 people combined. EXITS: 40+ smaller firms have gone bankrupt, been acquired or exited since 2023. DEPLOYMENT: China installed a record 315 GW of solar in 2025; H1 2026 additions collapsed to 72.07 GW, down ~66% from 212.21 GW in H1 2025; CPIA forecasts 180-240 GW for full-year 2026 — the first annual decline since 2019. BNEF cut its 2026 global forecast to 649 GW versus 690 GW in 2025 — the first annual contraction in records going back to 2000. EXPORTS: US$17.18 billion of wafers, cells and modules exported in H1 2026, +24.3% year-on-year in value, with cell exports +36.8% but module export volumes -2.5% — i.e. the chain is shifting from finished modules to cells shipped to offshore assembly. BATTERIES: Chinese lithium-ion capacity passed 2 TWh in 2024, about 60% above total demand; planned national capacity is approaching 5,000 GWh implying utilisation below 40%; power-battery planned capacity ~4,800 GWh against ~1,000 GWh demand (utilisation ~50-55%); stationary storage cell production in 2025 reached ~557 GWh, more than double global storage installations. LFP cell prices fell from ~US$110/kWh in early 2023 to ~US$50-60/kWh by late 2024; sodium-ion cells reached US$50-56/kWh in 2026 (BYD's third-generation NFPP at RMB 0.36-0.38/Wh). CONCENTRATION: CATL 43.42% and BYD 21.58% of China installations (CR2 ~65%); CATL 39.2% global share in 2025 with net profit of RMB 72.2 billion; China controls ~69% of the global EV battery market; the number of firms with meaningful domestic vehicle-battery installations fell to record lows of 33 in January and 30 in February 2026, with the top 10 taking 94.1%. STORAGE DEPLOYMENT: China's cumulative new-type energy storage reached 144.7 GW at end-2025, a 45-fold increase over the end of the 13th Five-Year Plan, with a 2025-2027 action plan targeting over 180 GW by 2027 and ~RMB 250 billion of direct project investment.
fase_tren_di_china: Split by layer. MANUFACTURING: late-stage backlash / forced consolidation — a regulated shakeout. The sector is loss-making, politically designated as the flagship case of 'involution' (内卷), and is being restructured by administrative means (energy-consumption standards, capacity-buyout fund, consumption taxes, below-cost pricing bans). Expect two to three more years of attrition before profitability normalises; Chinese analysts describe 2026 as the 'decisive/攻坚 year' of anti-involution and the possible profit inflection point. DOMESTIC DEPLOYMENT: mature and now contracting for the first time since 2019 as the guaranteed feed-in tariff was replaced by market-based pricing. STORAGE: still booming — the one genuinely growing segment, with utilisation of leading storage lines above 80% since Q2 2025, though stationary-storage cell capacity is itself now over-built. EXPORT/OFFSHORING: booming — capacity relocation to Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Latin America is accelerating precisely because domestic returns have collapsed. TECHNOLOGY: still advancing rapidly (TOPCon to BC and perovskite tandem; LFP to sodium-ion and solid-state), so the shakeout is not a technology stagnation, it is a margin collapse.
puncak_tren_china: Different peaks for different layers. Manufacturing capex and employment peaked in 2022-2023: solar-sector headcount across listed firms topped out at 776,750 in 2023, and capacity announcements peaked in 2022-2023 in Sichuan, Yunnan, Inner Mongolia, Qinghai and Xinjiang (the polysilicon belt, sited for cheap hydro and coal power) plus Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Anhui and Jiangxi for cells/modules. Module and polysilicon prices peaked in late 2021/2022 and have fallen continuously since. Domestic installation peaked in 2025 at 315 GW — an artificial rush-to-install ahead of the 1 June 2025 pricing reform, with H1 2025 alone reaching 212.21 GW; that spike is very unlikely to be repeated, making 2025 the deployment peak on current forecasts. Battery manufacturing capex peaked in 2022-2023 (Fujian/Ningde, Sichuan/Yibin, Jiangsu/Changzhou, Guangdong/Shenzhen-Huizhou, Hubei/Yichang), with a long tail of announced projects still being cancelled. The 'New Three' export value peaked in 2023 and has been falling in unit-price terms since, even where volumes still grow.
status_di_indonesia: MIXED / SPLIT. Deployment: barely started — Indonesia had roughly 1.49 GW of cumulative installed solar capacity in early 2026, less than 0.5% of what China added in 2025 alone. Manufacturing: just started and almost entirely Chinese-owned and export-oriented — around 3.2 GW/year of module capacity across four facilities, now hit by US anti-dumping duties. Batteries: pilot to early-commercial — one operating cell plant (HLI Green Power) and one large CATL-anchored project completing in 2026. Overcapacity cycle: ALREADY ARRIVED, but through nickel rather than solar — Indonesia is currently living through its own RKEF/NPI overcapacity bust, with smelters idling and layoffs, at the same time as China's solar bust. So Indonesia is a deep laggard in deployment, a beginner in manufacturing, and a simultaneous participant in the overcapacity cycle.
contoh_konkret_indonesia: MANUFACTURING: PT Trina Mas Agra Indonesia (TMAI) in the Kendal SEZ, Central Java — a joint venture of Trina Solar, Sinar Mas Group's Dian Swastatika Sentosa, PLN Indonesia Power Renewable and Agra Surya Energy — inaugurated as Indonesia's largest integrated cell-and-module plant, 1 GW/year initially with a 3 GW target, investment over Rp1.5 trillion. SEG Solar's Batang Industrial Park complex in Central Java — first high-efficiency n-type cell rolled off the line on 29 April 2025, targeting 5 GW cell / 3 GW module capacity, plus a 3 GW ingot-and-wafer facility (~US$80 million, production from Q3 2026), the first upstream wafer capacity in Southeast Asia outside China. LONGi announced a ~1.4 GW/year module plant near Jakarta in June 2025. BATTERIES: PT HLI Green Power (Hyundai Motor Group + LG Energy Solution) in Karawang, West Java — Indonesia's first EV battery cell plant, operating since July 2024, ~Rp13.5 trillion invested, ~10 GWh with a stated path to 30 GWh. The CATL-Antam-IBC 'Dragon/Titan' integrated project — US$5.9-6 billion, groundbreaking 29-30 June 2025, comprising nickel mining and HPAL in East Halmahera (North Maluku) plus a Karawang cell plant with 6.9 GWh initial capacity scaling to 15 GWh, targeted for launch around mid-to-late 2026, with about 8,000 direct jobs claimed. A parallel Antam-IBC-Huayou consortium battery ecosystem is slated for groundbreaking in H1 2026. DEPLOYMENT: the 192 MWp Cirata floating PV plant (Masdar-PLN) remains the flagship utility project; 2025 commissioning was led by the 50 MW Nusantara (IKN) and 25 MW East Bali plants. PLN's GIGA ONE tender for 1,225 MW of utility-scale solar opened on 30 April 2026 (Java 600 MW, Kalimantan 340 MW, Maluku-Papua 120 MW, West Nusa Tenggara 80 MW, Sulawesi 50 MW, Sumatra 35 MW). Sembcorp has launched a solar-plus-BESS project with PLN. POLICY: President Prabowo's 100 GW solar programme, announced August 2025 over five years and compressed to three years in May 2026, of which 80 GW is to be built as 1 MW solar plus 4 MWh BESS units in 80,000 villages (320 GWh of storage) managed by Koperasi Desa Merah Putih (KDMP).
data_skala_indonesia: INSTALLED SOLAR: ~1.49 GW cumulative as of early 2026. Rooftop solar was only ~479 MWac (~600 MWp) by end-2025, far below the 3.6 GW national strategic project target for 2025. The rooftop quota system allocates 5,746 MW across 11 grids for 2024-2028 (901 MW in 2024, 1,004 MW in 2025, 1,065 MW in 2026, 1,183 MW in 2027, 1,593 MW in 2028), but actual uptake has run far below quota. RUPTL 2025-2034 commits to 17.1 GW of solar within 69.5 GW of new capacity, ~76% of which is renewables and storage, and 42.6 GW of new renewable capacity in total. RENEWABLE SHARE: 14.65% in 2024, 15.75% in 2025, reported at 17.89% by April 2026; the original 23%-by-2025 target was abandoned and cut to 17-19%. PLN's roadmap: 15.9% (2025) to 21% (2030) to 34.3% (2034). POWER SYSTEM: PLN installed capacity ~46.8 GW at end-2024; electricity consumption ~1,584 kWh per capita in 2025 (+12% year-on-year) — roughly one-sixth of China's level. GDP per capita ~US$5,074-5,082 in 2025. MANUFACTURING: domestic module output ~3.2 GW/year across four facilities; the Ministry of Investment claims US$1.4 billion of FDI secured toward up to 50 GW of eventual local capacity [uncertain]. TRADE SHOCK: the US Department of Commerce set preliminary anti-dumping duties in April 2026 of 35.17% on Indonesia (India 123.04%, Laos 22.46%); combined with countervailing duties, Indonesian rates run roughly 121-178%. India, Indonesia and Laos together supplied US$4.5 billion of US solar imports in 2025, about two-thirds of volume. BATTERIES/NICKEL: nickel fell from over US$48,000/tonne in early 2022 to about US$15,000/tonne by July 2025; LME inventories rose above 250,000 tonnes; Indonesian RKEF smelter utilisation dropped to ~76%; PT Gunbuster Nickel Industry delayed US$47 million in supplier payments and idled 18 of its 22 furnaces in March 2025; Nickel Industries Ltd's EBITDA margin went from 34% (2022) to -7% (2024). The 2026 ore quota was cut to 250-270 million wet tonnes from ~379 million in 2025 (about -30%), pushing LME nickel back to US$20,000/tonne on 6 May 2026, with the government explicitly targeting a US$18,000-20,000 band. Only 8 Indonesian smelters produce battery-grade MHP; converting more NPI furnaces is estimated to need ~US$2.1 billion. EMPLOYMENT IN THE ECOSYSTEM: IMIP employs ~86,000 Indonesians, ~16,000 Chinese workers and ~24,000 contractors across 53 companies; IWIP had absorbed over 81,000 Indonesian workers by early 2025 and targets 100,000; Central Sulawesi hosts 35 smelters (22 in IMIP) and North Maluku 32 (19 in IWIP); Chinese companies control roughly 65% of Indonesia's refining capacity. Regional minimum wage around the nickel parks is ~Rp4 million (~US$244)/month. COOPERATIVE ROLLOUT: only about 1,061 KDMP village cooperatives were operational against a target of 80,000 — roughly 1%.
estimasi_lag_tahun: Layer-dependent, and this is the analytically important point. (1) SOLAR DEPLOYMENT: 12-15 years. Indonesia's ~1.49 GW cumulative in early 2026 is roughly where China stood in 2011-2012 (China passed ~3 GW cumulative in 2011 and ~20 GW in 2014). On a per-capita basis the gap is wider still: China has roughly 0.7-0.8 kW of solar per person versus Indonesia's ~0.005 kW — a factor of well over 100. (2) SOLAR MANUFACTURING SCALE: 15-18 years in volume (Indonesia's ~3.2 GW/year is China's 2008-2009 scale) but only 0-2 years in technology vintage, since Indonesian plants are being built directly with n-type TOPCon and, at SEG Batang, upstream ingot/wafer capability. (3) BATTERY CELL MANUFACTURING: 10-12 years. Indonesia's ~10 GWh operating capacity approximates China's 2014-2015 level; China now has roughly 100x that. (4) BESS DEPLOYMENT: 8-10 years — China's new-type storage was in the low single-digit GW in 2017-2018 and is now 144.7 GW; Indonesia's grid-scale BESS is essentially at zero commissioned capacity. (5) THE OVERCAPACITY CYCLE ITSELF: ZERO-TO-NEGATIVE LAG. Indonesia's nickel RKEF/NPI overcapacity bust (2024-2026) is running concurrently with China's solar and battery bust, and is partly caused by it — the same Chinese capital that built solar factories in Jiangsu built RKEF lines in Morowali on the same 'expand to win share' logic. Indonesia therefore does not have 12 years of grace before the overcapacity lesson becomes relevant; the lesson is already overdue. Net headline figure for the domain: approximately 12 years lag in deployment, 10-15 years in manufacturing scale, 0 years in exposure to the boom-bust cycle.
bukti_historical_lag: (a) COAL POWER: Indonesia followed China's coal build-out with roughly a 10-15 year lag and is now repeating China's oversupply outcome — the Java-Bali grid is oversupplied, coal plants run at falling capacity factors, coal sector revenue fell 21% to US$11.97 billion, and the government is cutting output to 600 million tonnes in 2026 to defend prices, exactly the administrative supply-control playbook China used on coal in 2016. (b) NICKEL DOWNSTREAMING: Indonesia's 2020 ore export ban and RKEF build-out replicated China's 2005-2015 stainless/NPI expansion at roughly a 10-year lag, and produced the same terminal condition — prices collapsing from US$48,000/t to US$15,000/t, smelters idling, and the state resorting to quota controls. This is the single strongest empirical support for the thesis that Indonesian downstreaming will hit a Chinese-style overcapacity wall. (c) EV TWO-WHEELERS AND FOUR-WHEELERS: Indonesia's EV market in 2024-2026 approximates China's 2015-2017 penetration, a 9-10 year lag, with Chinese brands (Wuling, BYD, Chery) leading the market rather than local incumbents. (d) SOLAR MANUFACTURING FOR EXPORT: Indonesia is repeating the exact Malaysia/Vietnam/Thailand/Cambodia sequence of 2015-2024 — Chinese firms relocate assembly to a tariff-free jurisdiction, build export capacity far above local demand, and are then hit by US AD/CVD within 2-4 years. Indonesia's 2024-2026 experience compressed that cycle to about two years, which is evidence that transmission lags are SHORTENING. (e) ROOFTOP SOLAR POLICY: Indonesia abolished net metering in January 2024 (MEMR Reg 2/2024) — China abandoned generous distributed-PV subsidies in stages from 2018 (the '531' policy) after over-subscription; Indonesia reached the same policy destination six years later but arrived there from under-deployment rather than over-deployment, which is a different and more damaging failure mode.
tipe_lag: HYBRID — the single most important framing for this domain. (1) LAGGARD on deployment and installed base (12-15 years behind, and losing ground annually in absolute terms). (2) LAGGARD-BUT-COMPRESSED on manufacturing: Indonesia enters at the technology frontier (TOPCon, LFP, HPAL/MHP) but at a fraction of scale and without upstream polysilicon, so it inherits the frontier's thin margins without the frontier's cost base. (3) SIMULTANEOUS on the overcapacity/commodity-bust cycle: Indonesia's nickel bust is contemporaneous with, and causally linked to, China's solar/battery bust. (4) POTENTIAL LEAPFROG on system architecture: because Indonesia has almost no legacy distributed solar and a genuinely archipelagic grid, it can go straight to solar-plus-storage microgrids and skip the sequence China went through (subsidised centralised solar, then curtailment crisis, then retrofit storage). The 100 GW / 80,000-village 1 MW + 4 MWh design is exactly such a leapfrog on paper. (5) REVERSE in one narrow sense: Indonesia controls the upstream nickel resource and is ahead of China in HPAL/MHP capacity siting, so on the raw-material node Indonesia is a price-setter, not a follower — this is Indonesia's only real leverage in the entire chain.
probabilitas_transfer: VERY HIGH (near-certain) for the hardware, deployment and Chinese-capital dimensions; HIGH for the overcapacity/price-war dynamic in nickel-battery downstreaming; MEDIUM for a full Chinese-style domestic solar-manufacturing overcapacity crisis, because Indonesia's solar factories are too few and too export-dependent to build the kind of national-scale glut China created.
alasan_probabilitas: Five reinforcing drivers. (1) PRICE: modules below RMB 1/W and LFP cells at US$50-60/kWh mean solar-plus-storage is now cheaper than diesel in every Indonesian outer-island system and is approaching parity with new coal on the main grids — the economics arrive whether or not policy is ready. (2) CHINESE CAPITAL IS ACTIVELY SEEKING EXITS: with domestic utilisation below 60% (polysilicon) and below 40-55% (batteries), and with Beijing taxing and restricting domestic expansion from September 2026, Chinese firms have overwhelming incentive to build offshore. Indonesia offers nickel, cheap land, SEZ incentives, 280 million people and non-alignment. Trina, LONGi, SEG, CATL, Huayou and Lygend have all already moved. (3) STATE DEMAND PULL: Prabowo's 100 GW-in-three-years programme, accelerated after the May 2026 rolling blackouts, creates the largest single procurement opportunity in Southeast Asian solar history and will be supplied overwhelmingly by Chinese hardware. (4) TARIFF ARBITRAGE: the US AD/CVD net has now closed on Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam and, from 2026, India, Indonesia and Laos — but relocation continues because each new jurisdiction buys 2-4 years of duty-free access. Indonesia's role as a relocation target is structural. (5) PRECEDENT: Indonesia has already absorbed the Chinese overcapacity model wholesale in nickel, where Chinese firms control ~65% of refining capacity and the boom-bust cycle has already played out. The one dampener: Indonesia's domestic solar demand (~1-3 GW/year) is an order of magnitude too small to absorb 50 GW of announced manufacturing ambition, so the risk is not a domestic glut of Indonesian-made panels — it is stranded, export-dependent factories that go idle the moment a trade case lands, which is precisely what the April 2026 duties threaten.
vektor_transmisi: (a) DIRECT ENTRY BY CHINESE PLAYERS — the dominant vector, and unusually explicit here. Trina Solar into Kendal SEZ via JV with Sinar Mas and PLN Indonesia Power; SEG Solar into Batang with 5 GW cell / 3 GW module / 3 GW ingot-wafer; LONGi with a ~1.4 GW module plant near Jakarta; CATL with Brunp Recycling and Lygend Resources into Karawang and East Halmahera in a US$6 billion integrated project alongside Antam and IBC; Huayou Cobalt in a parallel consortium; Tsingshan and Jiangsu Delong already controlling the nickel base. Chinese firms hold roughly 65% of Indonesian nickel refining capacity. (b) HARDWARE AND EQUIPMENT EXPORT — even where the factory is Indonesian-branded, the production equipment, the cell technology, the inverters (Huawei and Sungrow are global No.1 and No.2), the BESS containers and the EPC know-how are Chinese. Every megawatt Indonesia installs deepens the dependency. (c) TARIFF-DRIVEN CAPACITY RELOCATION — the Alliance for American Solar Manufacturing and Trade petitioned in July 2025 explicitly alleging that manufacturers moved to India, Indonesia and Laos to escape duties on Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam. This is a policy-created transmission vector: US trade action pushes Chinese capacity into Indonesia. (d) STATE-TO-STATE AND SOE FINANCE — Belt and Road-linked lending, Chinese policy-bank credit for smelters and industrial parks, and Indonesian SOE partnerships (PLN Indonesia Power, Antam, IBC, Danantara) that de-risk Chinese entry. (e) LOCAL COPYCAT AND CONGLOMERATE CAPITAL — Sinar Mas, Adaro, Barito Pacific, Salim, Bakrie and Djarum-linked vehicles entering solar/BESS with Chinese technology partners rather than building indigenous capability. (f) POLICY IMITATION — the Indonesian government has explicitly borrowed the Chinese downstreaming template (raw-material export ban, forced value-add, industrial parks, national champions), which means it is also importing the Chinese failure mode. The 2026 nickel ore quota cut to 250-270 Mt is a direct copy of China's supply-side structural reform toolkit. (g) DIASPORA AND HUMAN CAPITAL — a substantial Chinese expatriate technical workforce (~16,000 at IMIP alone) transferring process know-how, alongside Indonesian engineers trained in Chinese firms and, increasingly, Indonesian students on Chinese government scholarships in energy engineering. (h) ALGORITHMIC/CONTENT DIFFUSION — a minor but real vector: Chinese solar and BESS suppliers sell direct to Indonesian installers and prosumers via Alibaba, Made-in-China and TikTok Shop, seeding a grey-market rooftop and off-grid segment below the regulator's line of sight.
prasyarat_struktural: THRESHOLDS AND INDONESIA'S POSITION VERSUS CHINA AT COMPARABLE MOMENTS. (1) ELECTRICITY DEMAND GROWTH. Solar scales only where load is growing. China's power demand grew 8-10%/year through the 2010s; Indonesia's grew ~5-6% with consumption at just 1,584 kWh per capita in 2025 versus China's ~7,000 kWh. Worse, the Java-Bali grid is currently OVERSUPPLIED with take-or-pay coal PPAs, meaning new solar displaces contracted coal that PLN must pay for anyway. This is the single hardest structural constraint: without demand growth (data centres, EVs, electric cooking, industrial electrification, smelters shifted onto the grid) there is no room for 100 GW of solar regardless of price. (2) GRID AND STORAGE. China's solar boom was underwritten by the world's largest UHV transmission build-out plus, later, 144.7 GW of storage. Indonesia has no inter-island backbone, and its 100 GW plan implicitly acknowledges this by making 80 GW distributed. Prerequisite: BESS at scale and a functioning distribution grid in 80,000 villages — neither exists. (3) UTILITY FINANCIAL HEALTH AND OFFTAKE CREDIBILITY. PLN's monopsony, its subsidy-distorted tariffs and its history of not signing PPAs (the diesel-replacement programme announced in 2022 still has no signed PPAs) is the binding constraint. China's boom rode on a state-guaranteed feed-in tariff; Indonesia has no equivalent. (4) COST OF CAPITAL. Solar is a capex-front-loaded asset, so WACC dominates LCOE. Chinese developers financed at 3-5%; Indonesian projects face 9-13% rupiah rates plus currency risk, which can add 40-60% to levelised cost and erases much of the module price collapse. This is the most under-appreciated prerequisite. (5) GDP PER CAPITA AND AFFORDABILITY FOR ROOFTOP. China's distributed solar boom took off around 2017-2018 when GDP per capita was ~US$8,800-9,900 and household electricity prices were unsubsidised. Indonesia is at ~US$5,080 with heavily subsidised residential tariffs for the 450 VA-1,300 VA classes, so rooftop payback is structurally poor for the majority and only works for commercial/industrial customers on higher tariffs. Rule of thumb: mass residential rooftop needs either GDP/capita above ~US$8,000 or tariff reform — Indonesia has neither and is roughly 8-12 years from the income threshold at current growth. (6) MINERAL AND MANUFACTURING BASE. Indonesia has nickel (world's largest, ~50%+ of global mined supply) but no polysilicon, no metallurgical-grade silicon industry at scale, no lithium, and limited high-purity chemicals — so 'vertical integration' in solar stops at wafers, and in batteries stops at MHP/precursor. (7) INDUSTRIAL ELECTRICITY PRICE. Polysilicon is electro-intensive; China sited it in Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia, Sichuan and Yunnan for sub-US$0.03/kWh power. Indonesian industrial power is ~US$0.06-0.08/kWh, which makes upstream polysilicon in Indonesia structurally uncompetitive — a hard, probably permanent ceiling. (8) ABSORPTIVE DOMESTIC MARKET. China's manufacturers survived the 2013 bust because domestic installation exploded from 2013-2015. Indonesia has no such backstop: 3.2 GW of factories versus ~1-3 GW/year of domestic demand means Indonesian solar manufacturing is a pure export play, and therefore hostage to the trade policy of a single customer.
indikator_pemantauan: LEADING INDICATORS OF ARRIVAL/ACCELERATION: (1) Signed PPAs, not announcements — track how many of PLN's GIGA ONE 1,225 MW tender lots reach financial close, and whether the long-stalled diesel-replacement PPAs are finally executed. Zero-to-few signed PPAs after a tender is the reliable Indonesian failure signature. (2) Number of operational KDMP village cooperatives with an energised 1 MW + 4 MWh unit (currently ~1,061 cooperatives exist but essentially none with energy assets); crossing 5,000 energised units would mark genuine take-off. (3) BKPM/Ministry of Investment approvals (izin usaha) and new company registrations under KBLI codes for PV cell/module manufacturing, battery cell manufacturing and BESS integration — plus how many are Chinese-controlled. (4) Trade data: HS 8541.43 (PV cells/modules) and HS 8507.60 (lithium-ion) import and export volumes; a widening export/import gap signals the export-platform model, a narrowing one signals genuine domestic absorption. (5) Outcome of the US AD/CVD final determinations (final Indonesia deadline 13 July 2026) and any subsequent EU or Indian trade action — this determines whether Kendal and Batang run or idle. (6) Idle-capacity signals in nickel: RKAB ore quota decisions, RKEF utilisation (currently ~76%), furnace idling announcements, and PHK (layoff) filings with Disnaker in Morowali and Weda Bay. (7) Tariff and regulatory triggers: any reinstatement of net metering or introduction of a solar feed-in tariff; revision of TKDN thresholds (60% nominal, ESDM proposal to cut to 40%, plus the April 2025 project-differentiated exemption for projects with over 50% foreign financing); publication of the BESS regulation trailed for 2026. (8) Job postings on Jobstreet/LinkedIn Indonesia for 'PV design engineer', 'BESS engineer', 'SCADA/EMS', 'O&M solar', 'battery process engineer', 'electrochemistry', 'HPAL process' — currently in the low hundreds; a jump into the thousands is a real leading indicator. (9) University supply-side: new prodi approvals for Teknik Energi Terbarukan, Teknik Metalurgi, Teknik Elektro with power-electronics concentration, and any new battery/electrochemistry programme; also Chinese-government scholarship placements in energy engineering. (10) Trademark and brand registrations at DJKI by Chinese solar/battery brands (Trina, LONGi, Jinko, Sungrow, Huawei FusionSolar, CATL, EVE, Hithium, Deye, Growatt) — historically a 12-24 month leading indicator of market entry. (11) Grey-market signal: search volume and TikTok Shop/Tokopedia listings for 'panel surya', 'inverter hybrid', 'baterai LiFePO4' — the off-grid consumer segment moves before the regulated one. (12) Danantara's allocation decisions on energy — the sovereign fund's first large solar/BESS commitment would be a step-change signal.
hambatan_transfer: (1) PLN's monopsony and its structural conflict of interest: PLN owns coal generation and is locked into take-or-pay coal PPAs, so every megawatt of IPP solar is a cost to PLN, not a revenue. This has produced a two-decade pattern of ambitious targets and unsigned contracts. (2) Grid oversupply on Java-Bali coexisting with shortage and blackouts elsewhere (the May 2026 rolling blackouts) — a distribution and reliability problem that solar alone cannot solve and that BESS makes expensive. (3) Abolition of net metering (MEMR Reg 2/2024) plus a hard quota system, which killed rooftop economics and cut the most decentralised, least-capital-intensive growth path. (4) TKDN whiplash: a 60% local-content requirement from January 2025 that domestic industry cannot physically meet, then partial relaxation, then project-differentiated exemptions — policy instability that deters both manufacturers and developers. (5) Cost of capital: 9-13% rupiah financing plus FX mismatch (revenue in IDR, equipment in USD) versus 3-5% in China. (6) Land acquisition, permitting and the sheer administrative friction of building 80,000 village systems through cooperatives that mostly do not yet function. (7) Subsidised electricity tariffs that make solar look expensive to households even when it is cheap in real terms. (8) Fossil-fuel political economy: coal is Indonesia's largest export earner and is politically entrenched at national and provincial level; the 2026 output cut to 600 Mt is about defending coal prices, not about transition. (9) Human capital: acute shortage of PV design, protection-coordination, power-electronics, EMS/SCADA and battery-process engineers. (10) US and prospective EU trade action against Indonesian-assembled modules, which undermines the only viable business case for the factories now being built. (11) Nickel-sector distress, which is draining the fiscal and political appetite for further downstreaming bets exactly when battery investment needs support.
faktor_pembatal_transfer: CONDITIONS THAT MEAN THIS WILL NOT ARRIVE IN THE CHINESE FORM. (1) NO UPSTREAM POLYSILICON, AND PROBABLY NEVER. Polysilicon is the most electricity-intensive step in the chain; China built it on sub-US$0.03/kWh stranded hydro and coal power in Xinjiang, Yunnan, Sichuan and Inner Mongolia. Indonesia's industrial power runs roughly 2-3x that and its metallurgical-grade silicon base is negligible. Indonesia can plausibly reach wafers (SEG's Batang project) but the true value and true overcapacity risk sits upstream, where Indonesia will not compete. Indonesian 'solar sovereignty' therefore stops at assembly. (2) DOMESTIC MARKET TOO SMALL TO CREATE A CHINESE-STYLE GLUT. China's overcapacity was possible because 30+ provinces each subsidised local champions into a single unified national market. Indonesia has one buyer (PLN), a fragmented archipelagic grid, and 1-3 GW/year of demand. Indonesia will get STRANDED EXPORT FACTORIES, not a domestic price war — a different pathology requiring a different policy response. (3) THE ARCHIPELAGO INVERTS THE ECONOMICS. China's model was giant centralised plants in the desert west plus UHV lines to the coast. Indonesia has no equivalent geography and cannot build UHV across seas economically, so utility-scale-plus-transmission is structurally unavailable. The Indonesian form must be distributed and storage-heavy, which is more expensive per kWh, more operationally demanding, and far harder to finance — but also more valuable, because it displaces diesel at US$0.20-0.30/kWh. (4) NO STATE-DIRECTED CREDIT MACHINE. China's build-out rested on at least US$43 billion of policy-bank credit from 2009 onward and local governments willing to absorb losses. Indonesia's fiscal space is constrained, PLN is already subsidy-dependent, and Danantara's mandate is contested. Indonesia cannot buy its way through a loss-making decade the way China did. (5) LABOUR COST ADVANTAGE IS NOT DECISIVE. Modern TOPCon and LFP lines are highly automated — labour is a single-digit share of cost. Indonesia's cheap labour therefore does not offset its expensive power, expensive capital and thin supplier ecosystem. This is the core reason Indonesia cannot become 'the next China' in solar manufacturing regardless of policy. (6) TIMING: INDONESIA IS ENTERING A CONTRACTING GLOBAL MARKET. BNEF cut 2026 global solar to 649 GW versus 690 GW in 2025 — the first annual contraction on record. Entering manufacturing at a global demand peak, with a Chinese incumbent operating at 60% utilisation and pricing at cash cost, is the worst possible entry timing. (7) TRADE WALLS ARE CLOSING FASTER THAN CAPACITY CAN BE BUILT. Indonesia went from relocation destination to 121-178% combined US duties in roughly two years. Any future Indonesian solar export platform faces the same fate within a similar window, meaning the export-platform model has a structurally short half-life. (8) BATTERY CHEMISTRY IS MOVING AWAY FROM NICKEL. LFP has already taken the majority of the market and sodium-ion reached US$50-56/kWh in 2026, approaching parity with lithium. Indonesia's entire downstreaming thesis is built on nickel demand from NCM chemistries that are losing share. This is the most serious cancellation risk of all: Indonesia may complete a nickel-battery value chain just as the world stops needing nickel in batteries.
tahun_masuk_indonesia: Already arrived, in three distinct entries: manufacturing in 2024-2025 (Trina Kendal, SEG Batang first cell 29 April 2025, LONGi announcement June 2025), battery cells in July 2024 (HLI Green Power) with the CATL-Antam-IBC complex following in 2025-2026, and the overcapacity/price-collapse dynamic in 2023-2025 via nickel. The policy-demand entry point is August 2025 (Prabowo's 100 GW announcement), sharply accelerated by the May 2026 blackouts and the subsequent compression of the timeline to three years.
tahun_mainstream_indonesia: 2029-2032 for solar-plus-storage as a normal, non-exotic part of Indonesian electricity supply — i.e. multi-gigawatt annual additions, BESS as a standard tender component, and solar visible in ordinary commercial and industrial buildings. The gating items are PPA execution discipline at PLN, a workable BESS regulatory and tariff framework (trailed for 2026), and either tariff reform or a rooftop incentive that replaces net metering. For rooftop/residential mainstreaming specifically, 2032-2037 is more realistic given the income threshold and subsidised tariffs. For domestic battery manufacturing to be mainstream (multiple plants, local supply chain, Indonesian-made cells in Indonesian vehicles and BESS), 2030-2033. The 100 GW-in-three-years target (i.e. by 2029) should be treated as a political aspiration with a very low probability of being met on time — the KDMP delivery vehicle is at ~1% readiness — but even 20-30% delivery would represent a transformational 20-30 GW.
tahun_puncak_indonesia: Two peaks to distinguish. (a) DEPLOYMENT PEAK: not before the mid-2030s; on a plausible trajectory Indonesian annual solar additions peak somewhere around 2035-2040 at perhaps 10-20 GW/year, constrained by load growth rather than by hardware cost. (b) MANUFACTURING/INVESTMENT PEAK — much sooner and much sharper: 2026-2028. Announced solar factory capacity is already far above domestic demand and its export outlet is being closed by US duties, so the Indonesian solar-manufacturing investment cycle likely peaks around 2026-2027 and enters its own shakeout in 2028-2030 — a compressed replay of China's 2011-2013, but without a domestic demand backstop. (c) The NICKEL/BATTERY-MATERIAL peak has arguably already passed: the 2022 price peak and the 2023-2024 capex peak are behind, and the 2026 quota regime marks the transition from expansion to managed contraction. Expect an Indonesian 'anti-involution' moment in nickel and battery materials around 2027-2030.
skenario_percepatan: (1) Repeat blackouts — the May 2026 outages already compressed the 100 GW timeline from five years to three; another reliability crisis would trigger emergency procurement. (2) A functioning BESS regulation plus a bankable standardised PPA and PLN take-or-pay for solar. (3) Data-centre and AI load arriving in Indonesia with corporate 24/7 clean-power requirements — the fastest realistic demand-creation channel. (4) Diesel replacement executed: ~5-6 GW of diesel generation displaced by solar-plus-BESS is immediately economic and needs only contractual will. (5) Continued module and cell price collapse from Chinese overcapacity, plus sodium-ion reaching parity, cutting BESS capex sharply. (6) Danantara or a sovereign green-financing vehicle providing sub-7% long-tenor rupiah debt, which would do more for deployment than any hardware subsidy. (7) Carbon border measures (CBAM and successors) forcing Indonesian exporters — nickel, aluminium, textiles, palm derivatives — to buy renewable power. (8) Reinstatement of net metering or an equivalent export-credit scheme for rooftop.
dampak_lapangan_kerja: JOBS CREATED — installation, EPC and O&M is the largest and most geographically dispersed category: PV designers, protection and SCADA engineers, DC/AC electricians, mounting-structure fabricators, BESS commissioning technicians, drone and thermographic inspection crews, and long-tail O&M including panel cleaning (a real, recurring, low-skill job in a dusty tropical climate). A distributed 80 GW build would need on the order of 200,000-400,000 person-years of installation labour [uncertain], spread across all provinces rather than concentrated in Java. Manufacturing jobs are far fewer than advertised: modern TOPCon and LFP lines are heavily automated, so a 1 GW module plant employs only several hundred people; the CATL-Antam project claims ~8,000 direct jobs for a US$6 billion investment — about US$750,000 of capital per job, an order of magnitude worse than labour-intensive manufacturing. Battery and materials add electrochemists, HPAL process operators, precursor/cathode chemists, and battery-safety and recycling specialists. Cooperative-level roles emerge if the KDMP model works: village energy operators, meter and billing administrators, microgrid dispatchers. JOBS LOST OR TRANSFORMED — diesel genset supply, service and fuel logistics (a large informal economy in eastern Indonesia); coal-plant operations staff as capacity factors fall; and, more acutely, the nickel-smelting workforce as the RKEF cycle turns: IMIP's ~86,000 Indonesian workers, ~24,000 contractors, and IWIP's 81,000+ are exposed to a downturn that has already idled 18 of 22 furnaces at PT Gunbuster and driven RKEF utilisation to ~76%. Because these workers left farming and fishing to enter the smelters, layoffs convert directly into rural poverty rather than into re-employment. The Chinese precedent is stark: 154,543 solar jobs disappeared in a single year (2024) across 110 listed firms, and over 220,000 across the two-year downturn, with the top five firms cutting more than 30% of headcount. Indonesia should assume that new-energy manufacturing jobs are cyclical, not permanent, and that the durable employment is in installation, operations, maintenance and recycling — which cannot be offshored.
dampak_kelas_menengah: Mostly indirect, and asymmetric. POSITIVE: cheaper marginal electricity over time; a genuine asset-ownership opportunity for the upper-middle class and for commercial/industrial property owners, where rooftop solar plus a hybrid inverter yields 5-8 year paybacks on non-subsidised tariffs; new professional careers (PV design, energy management, ESG and carbon accounting, EPC project management) that pay above the national middle-class median; and a fast-growing SME segment in installation, distribution and O&M with low capital barriers. NEGATIVE / LIMITING: the abolition of net metering in January 2024 removed the main mechanism by which middle-class households could monetise rooftop solar, so the segment that would naturally adopt first has been deliberately fenced out; subsidised residential tariffs simultaneously make solar look unattractive, meaning the middle class pays for the subsidy through taxes while being denied the alternative. If the 100 GW programme is financed through PLN's balance sheet and ultimately the state budget, the middle class bears the fiscal cost of a programme whose benefits accrue mainly to rural electrification and to Chinese equipment suppliers. There is also a savings-and-investment channel: Indonesian retail investors are heavily exposed to nickel, coal and energy names on the IDX (ANTM, INCO, MDKA, NCKL, ADRO, PTBA, and battery-linked counters), so a downstreaming bust transmits directly into middle-class portfolios — the Chinese experience, where solar equities lost the bulk of their value from 2022 peaks, is the relevant warning. Finally, a middle-class energy-prosumer class of the kind that emerged in China, Vietnam and Australia will not form in Indonesia until either tariffs are reformed or net metering returns.
dampak_daerah_non_jawa: This is one of the few domains where the non-Java impact is LARGER than the Java impact, in both directions. UPSIDE: Indonesia's best solar resource and its worst electricity economics are both outside Java. Diesel-fired generation in NTT, Maluku, North Maluku, Papua and remote Kalimantan and Sulawesi costs US$0.20-0.30/kWh; solar-plus-BESS beats it decisively today. The 80 GW distributed component of the 100 GW plan is explicitly targeted at 80,000 villages, most of them outside Java, and the PLN GIGA ONE tender allocates 625 MW of its 1,225 MW outside Java (Kalimantan 340 MW, Maluku-Papua 120 MW, NTB 80 MW, Sulawesi 50 MW, Sumatra 35 MW). Reliable 24-hour electricity in eastern Indonesia would change cold-chain fisheries, agro-processing, health services and schooling more than any other single intervention. DOWNSIDE: the overcapacity risk is also concentrated outside Java. Central Sulawesi (35 smelters, 22 in IMIP) and North Maluku (32 smelters, 19 in IWIP) have built single-industry economies around nickel with ~86,000 and ~81,000 workers respectively; the current price crash, quota cuts and furnace idling threaten a regional depression in exactly the places with the thinnest social safety nets and where households abandoned farming and fishing to take smelter jobs. This is the Chinese 'resource city' problem (Xinyu in Jiangxi, where LDK Solar generated over 93% of the city's solar tax receipts before collapsing) reproduced in Indonesian form. Meanwhile solar MANUFACTURING is concentrated in Java (Kendal and Batang in Central Java, Karawang in West Java) and in SEZs, so the industrial jobs go to Java while the extraction risk sits in the outer islands — reinforcing rather than reducing the existing centre-periphery imbalance. Governance risk is also higher outside Java: 80,000 village cooperatives handling energy assets is an unprecedented decentralised procurement and maintenance challenge, and only ~1,061 KDMP are operational.
jurusan_terancam: Not 'threatened by obsolescence' so much as facing shrinking or volatile demand, and needing to be re-scoped rather than closed. (1) Teknik Perminyakan and Teknik Gas — flat-to-declining domestic upstream investment; graduates increasingly compete for a shrinking pool of conventional projects. (2) Teknik Pertambangan Batubara and coal-specific mining specialisations — Indonesia is capping output at 600 Mt in 2026 and coal revenue fell 21% to US$11.97 billion; the long-run trajectory is managed decline. (3) Teknik Mesin with a purely thermal/combustion focus (boilers, steam cycles, internal combustion) — the skills transfer poorly to power electronics and electrochemistry without deliberate retooling. (4) Teknik Metalurgi programmes narrowly built around pyrometallurgy and RKEF/NPI processing — this is the sharpest risk, because these programmes expanded specifically to serve the nickel boom and are now feeding a contracting employer base; hydrometallurgy and HPAL are where demand is shifting. (5) Teknik Elektro concentrations built around conventional generation and transmission protection without power-electronics, inverter and grid-forming content. (6) Administrative and clerical programmes attached to the fossil supply chain (logistics for coal barging, fuel distribution) in Kalimantan and Sumatra. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: the Chinese experience shows that new-energy programmes themselves can become the risk — Chinese universities mass-opened 新能源科学与工程 and 储能科学与工程 programmes during the boom, and their graduates entered a market that shed 154,543 jobs in 2024 alone. Indonesian universities that open narrow, single-technology 'solar' or 'battery' prodi risk producing an oversupplied cohort into the same cycle. The safest structure is a broad electrical/chemical/materials core with new-energy specialisation in the final years.
jurusan_dibutuhkan: (1) POWER ELECTRONICS AND GRID INTEGRATION — inverter design and control, grid-forming inverters, protection coordination in high-inverter-penetration systems, power quality, harmonics. This is the single scarcest skill in Indonesia and is required for every megawatt installed. (2) ENERGY STORAGE ENGINEERING — battery system design, BMS, thermal management, safety and fire engineering, EMS/dispatch optimisation, degradation modelling and warranty analytics. Indonesia currently has no dedicated undergraduate storage programme comparable to China's 储能科学与工程, which now runs at 114 institutions. (3) ELECTROCHEMISTRY AND MATERIALS — cathode/anode chemistry, precursor and CAM production, LFP and increasingly sodium-ion chemistry, solid-state fundamentals. (4) HYDROMETALLURGY AND HPAL PROCESS ENGINEERING — the specific chokepoint in Indonesia's battery-materials ambition, where only 8 smelters produce MHP and ~US$2.1 billion of retrofit investment is needed. (5) SYSTEM AND RESOURCE MODELLING — PVsyst/SAM, PLEXOS/production-cost modelling, resource assessment, curtailment and capacity-value analysis; power-system planning for archipelagic microgrids. (6) ENERGY FINANCE AND PROJECT STRUCTURING — PPA negotiation, project finance, FX and offtake risk, blended and concessional finance, carbon markets. Indonesia's binding constraint is bankability, not engineering, so this is arguably the highest-leverage discipline. (7) DATA AND AI FOR ENERGY — forecasting, digital twins, predictive O&M, drone/thermal inspection analytics. (8) BATTERY AND MODULE RECYCLING AND CIRCULAR ECONOMY — an entirely open field in Indonesia; China is already building this out through Brunp (a CATL subsidiary present in the Indonesian project). (9) OCCUPATIONAL SAFETY AND PROCESS SAFETY ENGINEERING — given 93 workplace accidents over eight years to 2023 at IMIP and the December 2023 furnace fire that killed 13 and injured 46, this is a moral as well as an economic priority. (10) VOCATIONAL (SMK/politeknik) — certified PV installers, DC electricians, BESS commissioning technicians, high-voltage safety. Volume matters more than prestige here: an 80,000-village programme is bottlenecked on certified technicians, not on PhDs.
china_education_response: China treated new-energy talent as an explicit industrial-policy instrument and moved fast in both directions. EXPANSION: the Ministry of Education created 新能源科学与工程 (New Energy Science and Engineering) as a Strategic Emerging Industry major in 2010-2011 and it spread to several hundred institutions; 储能科学与工程 (Energy Storage Science and Engineering) was created in 2020 at Xi'an Jiaotong University and by 2026 was offered at 114 institutions and, notably, was included in the 强基计划 (Strong Foundation Plan) elite admissions track for the first time in 2026 — a signal that storage is now treated as a strategic-scarcity discipline rather than a vocational one. The 2026 undergraduate catalogue added 38 new majors including 能源科学与工程 (Energy Science and Engineering) and 深地科学与工程, explicitly aligned to national strategic needs. Related additions across the period include 智慧能源工程, 氢能科学与工程, 碳储科学与工程 (carbon storage), and 资源循环科学与工程 (resource recycling). PRUNING: the same system withdraws aggressively. Across the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-2025) Chinese universities added 10,200 undergraduate programme points and withdrew or suspended 12,200 — a net contraction, with cumulative adjustment exceeding 30% of all programme points and the annual adjustment rate exceeding 10% for the first time. In the 2024 review alone, 1,839 programme points were added, 2,220 suspended and 1,428 withdrawn. VOCATIONAL LAYER: MOE and MOHRSS added photovoltaic system installation, energy storage O&M, and new-energy equipment technician occupations to the national vocational catalogue, and the 'new energy' cluster became one of the largest recruiting streams in secondary vocational schools. THE WARNING FOR INDONESIA: this responsiveness produced its own overshoot. Programme expansion peaked in 2021-2023, exactly as the industry peaked, and the resulting graduate cohorts entered a labour market that shed over 220,000 solar jobs. Chinese commentary through 2025-2026 openly discusses new-energy graduates struggling to find positions while firms simultaneously bid up AI talent. The lesson is not 'open new-energy programmes fast' — it is 'build broad engineering fundamentals with a new-energy specialisation layer that can be re-pointed when the cycle turns.'
respons_kebijakan_china: CHINA'S POST-HOC CORRECTION — the 'anti-involution' (反内卷) package, which is the most directly transferable policy content in this entire domain. (1) POLITICAL DESIGNATION: on 1 July 2025 the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission named disorderly low-price competition as a target, elevating anti-involution from industry complaint to national policy and writing it into the 15th Five-Year Plan. (2) BELOW-COST PRICING BAN: MIIT, NDRC and CPIA convened repeated CEO symposiums and required that bidding, procurement and sales not occur below cost — enforced through the amended Price Law and unfair-competition rules. (3) MANDATORY ENERGY-CONSUMPTION STANDARDS AS A CAPACITY FILTER: draft compulsory national standards on unit energy consumption for polysilicon (both Siemens/TCS and silane fluidised-bed routes) and germanium were issued for comment in September 2025, with mandatory efficiency standards effective 1 January 2027 — a legally clean, WTO-defensible way to force old lines to close without naming companies. (4) CAPACITY BUYOUT VEHICLE: Beijing Guanghe Qiancheng Technology was registered in December 2025, jointly held by leading polysilicon producers with an initial RMB 3 billion capital base and a proposed RMB 50 billion fund, endorsed by NDRC and MIIT, to acquire and permanently retire roughly one million tonnes of the ~3.5 million tonnes of polysilicon capacity — about one third. (5) CONSUMPTION TAXES ON THE PRODUCTS THEMSELVES: 2% on battery products from September 2026 rising to 4% from September 2027; 2% on PV cells from 1 April 2027 rising to 4% from 1 April 2028 — a deliberate margin squeeze designed to make marginal producers unviable. (6) REGULATORY SUMMONS: in January 2026 four agencies summoned 16 leading battery firms to warn against below-cost pricing and disorderly capacity build-out. (7) DEMAND-SIDE PRICING REFORM: the June 2025 shift to market-based pricing for renewable output (removing the guaranteed tariff), which caused the H1 2025 rush and the 2026 demand cliff — a cautionary example of badly sequenced reform. (8) THE LIMIT CASE: an attempt to form an explicit output-quota joint venture to absorb excess polysilicon was HALTED BY REGULATORS ON ANTITRUST GROUNDS — showing that even China cannot legally cartelise its way out, and that the durable instruments are standards, taxes and finance, not quotas. WHAT INDONESIA CAN ADOPT PREEMPTIVELY: capacity-approval discipline tied to signed offtake; mandatory energy and emissions intensity standards for smelters and any future cell/module plants set at frontier levels from day one; a below-cost-selling prohibition in public tenders; a sinking fund financed by the industry during good years to pay for closure, remediation and worker transition during bad ones; and a hard rule that state-linked finance (Danantara, Himbara banks) does not fund capacity expansion into an already over-supplied product.
rekomendasi_kebijakan_indonesia: (1) IMPOSE CAPACITY DISCIPLINE BEFORE THE GLUT, NOT AFTER. Make new smelter, cell and module capacity approvals conditional on contracted offtake and on a frontier energy-and-emissions-intensity standard, copying China's polysilicon energy-consumption instrument but applying it at entry rather than at exit. This is the single highest-value preemptive policy available, and Indonesia has already learned the cost of not having it in nickel. (2) BUILD THE COUNTERCYCLICAL FUND NOW. Levy a modest tonnage or capacity fee on nickel, battery-materials and PV manufacturing during price upswings into a ring-fenced fund for smelter closure, site remediation, and worker retraining and relocation — the mechanism China had to improvise at RMB 50 billion after the damage was done. Tie it explicitly to the Morowali and Weda Bay workforce. (3) SEQUENCE DEMAND BEFORE SUPPLY. Do not repeat China's Document 136 error in reverse: Indonesia is building factories without a demand mechanism. Fix the demand side first — a bankable standardised PPA, PLN take-or-pay obligations for tendered solar, and a firm timetable to convert take-or-pay coal contracts. (4) RESTORE A ROOFTOP EXPORT MECHANISM. The abolition of net metering under MEMR Reg 2/2024 was a self-inflicted wound; replace it with a transparent export-credit or feed-in-premium capped by grid-hosting capacity rather than by arbitrary quota. (5) STABILISE TKDN. Replace the oscillation between 60%, 40% and project-differentiated exemptions with a published multi-year local-content escalator tied to verified domestic capability, so manufacturers can plan. Unstable TKDN deters exactly the investment it is meant to attract. (6) DO NOT CHASE POLYSILICON. Indonesian industrial power costs make upstream polysilicon structurally uncompetitive; direct state support instead to wafer/cell (where SEG has moved), inverters and BESS integration, and above all to installation, O&M and recycling — the segments that cannot be offshored and that scale with domestic deployment. (7) DIVERSIFY OFF NICKEL DEPENDENCE IN THE BATTERY THESIS. LFP already dominates and sodium-ion reached US$50-56/kWh in 2026. Indonesia should actively court LFP and sodium-ion cell manufacturing for the domestic BESS market rather than betting the entire downstreaming programme on nickel-bearing chemistries. (8) NEGOTIATE TRADE EXPOSURE DELIBERATELY. With US preliminary duties at 121-178% combined, Indonesia should not licence further purely export-oriented module capacity without a demonstrated non-US market, and should pursue substantive local value-addition thresholds that survive origin scrutiny rather than assembly-only operations. (9) CONDITION FOREIGN INVESTMENT ON TECHNOLOGY AND HUMAN-CAPITAL TRANSFER. Require verified training quotas, Indonesian engineering leadership ratios, and local R&D spend in every SEZ incentive package, with clawbacks — Indonesia's nickel experience shows that jobs without capability transfer leave nothing behind when the cycle turns. (10) ENFORCE OCCUPATIONAL SAFETY AS A LICENCE CONDITION. 93 recorded workplace accidents over eight years to 2023 at IMIP, and 13 deaths in a single December 2023 furnace fire, are a policy failure, not an accident rate. (11) SEQUENCE THE 100 GW PROGRAMME REALISTICALLY. With ~1,061 of 80,000 KDMP operational, the village-cooperative delivery model is the binding constraint; build a professional operations-and-maintenance backbone (regional service companies with performance contracts) rather than assuming cooperatives can own, dispatch and maintain 320 GWh of batteries. (12) MANDATE END-OF-LIFE OBLIGATIONS FROM DAY ONE. Extended producer responsibility for modules and batteries, set before the first large decommissioning wave, is far cheaper than retrofitting it later.
peluang_bisnis: (1) EPC, INSTALLATION AND O&M — the largest, most defensible and least capital-intensive opportunity, and structurally impossible to import. A 100 GW programme, even at 25% delivery, implies tens of thousands of installations across all provinces. Regional O&M service companies with certified technicians and performance guarantees will be the durable winners. (2) BESS INTEGRATION AND SYSTEM ENGINEERING — importing Chinese cells and integrating locally (racks, enclosures, thermal management, fire suppression, EMS software, grid compliance) captures margin without competing on cell manufacturing, where Indonesia cannot win. This is the highest-value realistic manufacturing niche. (3) DIESEL REPLACEMENT AS A SERVICE — solar-plus-BESS displacing US$0.20-0.30/kWh diesel in eastern Indonesia is immediately profitable; the constraint is contracting, not economics. Energy-as-a-service and build-own-operate models for PLN's isolated systems, mining sites, plantations, telecom towers and island resorts are underserved. (4) COMMERCIAL AND INDUSTRIAL ROOFTOP — factories, cold storage, malls and hospitals on non-subsidised tariffs still deliver 5-8 year paybacks even without net metering, especially when paired with a small battery for peak shaving. Add CBAM-driven demand from exporters needing verifiable renewable supply. (5) MOUNTING STRUCTURES, CABLING, COMBINER BOXES, TRANSFORMERS AND BOS — genuinely localisable, high-weight, high-freight-cost components where Indonesian steel and electrical manufacturers have a natural advantage over imports. (6) FLOATING SOLAR — Indonesia's reservoir portfolio (Cirata proved the model at 192 MWp) plus land scarcity in Java makes FPV a structural niche with specialised anchoring, mooring and marine-electrical expertise. (7) BATTERY AND MODULE RECYCLING — no incumbent in Indonesia, a guaranteed feedstock stream from EVs, BESS and eventually modules, and a strategic hedge against nickel price volatility. Brunp (CATL's recycling arm) is already in the Karawang project, which signals both the opportunity and the competition. (8) SOFTWARE — EMS/SCADA for archipelagic microgrids, prepaid metering and billing for village cooperatives, and forecasting/dispatch optimisation; almost no Indonesian-built products exist and imported systems fit the cooperative model poorly. (9) TESTING, CERTIFICATION, INSURANCE AND ASSET ASSURANCE — independent engineering, performance testing (a real need given cheap imported hardware), warranty adjudication and specialist insurance for solar/BESS assets. (10) FINANCING PRODUCTS — rupiah-denominated long-tenor solar leases, cooperative lending, and receivables financing for installers; the binding constraint on the whole sector is capital cost, so whoever solves it captures disproportionate value. (11) BUYING DISTRESSED CHINESE HARDWARE — a genuine, time-limited arbitrage: with polysilicon utilisation below 60% and storage cell production at double global installations, Indonesian buyers are in the strongest procurement position in history and should be locking in long-dated supply agreements now.
rekomendasi_individu_mahasiswa: Build a broad, cycle-resistant core and specialise on top of it — do not bet a whole degree on one technology. (1) CORE: electrical engineering with real power-electronics depth (inverter topologies, control, grid-forming), or chemical/materials engineering with electrochemistry, or mechanical with thermal/fluids for HPAL and battery thermal management. (2) LAYER ON TOOLS: PVsyst, HelioScope or SAM for design; ETAP/DIgSILENT or PSS/E for grid studies; Python for data analysis, forecasting and O&M analytics; and basic SCADA/EMS familiarity. (3) GET CERTIFIED, NOT JUST DEGREED: BNSP competency certification for PV installation, K3 Listrik (electrical safety), and if possible international credentials (NABCEP-equivalent, IEC standards literacy). For an 80,000-village programme, a certified technician who can commission and troubleshoot is more immediately employable than a fresh S1 without field skills. (4) LEARN THE MONEY: energy project finance, PPA structure, LCOE and IRR modelling, FX and offtake risk. Indonesia's bottleneck is bankability; engineers who can speak to lenders are scarce and command a premium. (5) ADD A LANGUAGE AND A NETWORK: Mandarin is disproportionately valuable — Chinese firms dominate the equipment, the EPC know-how and increasingly the Indonesian plants; being the bridge between a Chinese technical team and an Indonesian regulator or utility is a career in itself. (6) CHOOSE THE NON-CYCLICAL SIDE OF THE INDUSTRY: manufacturing employment is volatile (China shed over 220,000 solar jobs in two years); installation, O&M, grid integration, safety and recycling grow with the installed base and are far more stable. (7) BUILD PORTFOLIO EVIDENCE: design and commission a real system — a campus rooftop, a village microgrid, a lab-scale BESS with a working EMS. In a young industry, demonstrated field competence beats credentials. (8) UNDERSTAND THE CYCLE ITSELF: read the Chinese case honestly. Anyone entering this sector should know what overcapacity does to employers, so they can read warning signs (utilisation rates, below-cost bidding, capex announcements outrunning demand) before their own employer runs into them.
rekomendasi_perguruan_tinggi: (1) DO NOT MASS-OPEN NARROW 'SOLAR' OR 'BATTERY' PRODI. China's cautionary example is decisive: it opened new-energy and storage programmes at scale exactly as the industry peaked and produced graduates into a market that lost 154,543 jobs in one year. Instead, create new-energy CONCENTRATIONS within existing Teknik Elektro, Teknik Kimia, Teknik Mesin and Teknik Metalurgi degrees, so the specialisation can be re-pointed when the cycle turns. (2) BUILD A STORAGE AND POWER-ELECTRONICS TRACK URGENTLY — this is the genuine national scarcity. Model it on the content of China's 储能科学与工程 (now at 114 institutions) but deliver it as a final-two-year concentration, covering BMS, thermal and fire safety, EMS/dispatch, degradation modelling and grid-forming inverter control. (3) PRIORITISE VOCATIONAL VOLUME OVER DEGREE PRESTIGE. The 100 GW programme is bottlenecked on certified installers and commissioning technicians, not on engineers. Politeknik Negeri (Jember, Ujung Pandang, Bandung, Semarang, Bali, Manado, Ambon, Kupang) and SMK networks should be funded to produce BNSP-certified PV and BESS technicians at scale, with mandatory field placement — and this capacity should be built in eastern Indonesia, where the installations will be. (4) EMBED PROJECT FINANCE AND POLICY INTO ENGINEERING CURRICULA. A required course on PPA structuring, LCOE, risk allocation and regulation would address Indonesia's actual constraint. (5) ESTABLISH SHARED TESTING AND CERTIFICATION LABS — PV module and BESS testing facilities co-funded by industry, serving both teaching and national quality assurance, which Indonesia currently lacks and will need badly as cheap imported hardware floods in. (6) STRENGTHEN HYDROMETALLURGY, NOT JUST PYROMETALLURGY, in metallurgy programmes at ITB, UI, Trisakti, UNHAS, Universitas Tadulako and Universitas Khairun — HPAL/MHP is where the battery value sits and where only 8 Indonesian plants currently operate. Site programmes near Morowali and Weda Bay. (7) OPEN RECYCLING AND CIRCULAR-ECONOMY CONTENT NOW, before the first decommissioning wave, since no Indonesian institution currently teaches battery or module recycling seriously. (8) MAKE PROCESS SAFETY A REQUIRED, EXAMINED SUBJECT in all metallurgy and battery programmes, given the recorded accident history in the nickel parks. (9) INSTITUTIONALISE PRUNING. Adopt China's discipline of periodically reviewing and closing programme points — the 14th Five-Year Plan saw 12,200 withdrawn or suspended against 10,200 added — so that Indonesian universities do not accumulate obsolete fossil-era programmes alongside new ones. (10) BUILD CHINA-FACING RESEARCH LINKS DELIBERATELY, with joint labs and staff exchange agreements that include IP and training clauses, so that the technology transfer Indonesia is paying for through FDI incentives actually reaches Indonesian institutions.
dampak_negatif_china: (1) MASS JOB DESTRUCTION IN A 'STRATEGIC' INDUSTRY. Listed solar company headcount fell from 776,750 (2023) to 622,207 (end-2024) — 154,543 jobs in twelve months — with more than 220,000 workers laid off or forced out of the industry over the two-year downturn and the top five firms cutting over 30% of staff. These were exactly the 'good' green jobs that the policy was meant to create. (2) CAPITAL DESTRUCTION AND BANKRUPTCY. Over 40 firms bankrupt, acquired or exited since 2023; aggregate listed-company losses above RMB 50 billion in 2025; entire polysilicon lines being bought purely to be scrapped. (3) LOCAL FISCAL COLLAPSE IN SINGLE-INDUSTRY CITIES. The LDK Solar precedent — the company generated over 93% of Xinyu city's solar tax receipts before failing — shows how a municipal budget can be hollowed out by one firm's collapse. (4) BANK AND SHADOW-CREDIT EXPOSURE from at least US$43 billion of policy-bank credit extended from 2009, much of it into capacity now being retired. (5) VALUE DESTRUCTION FOR RETAIL INVESTORS, who bought solar and battery equities at 2021-2022 peaks. (6) SUPPLIER-CHAIN DISTRESS — extended payment terms and forced acceptance of below-cost prices pushed losses down to smaller component and equipment suppliers who lacked the balance sheet to absorb them. (7) INNOVATION SUPPRESSION — with everyone selling below cost, R&D budgets were cut and the industry converged on commodity TOPCon rather than differentiating; Chinese commentary explicitly identifies involution as anti-innovative. (8) ENVIRONMENTAL COST — polysilicon production concentrated in coal-heavy Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia for cheap power, plus a growing module-waste problem and the reputational and trade consequences of Xinjiang supply-chain forced-labour allegations. (9) TRADE RETALIATION — US, EU, India and now Southeast Asian-transshipment duties, which have progressively closed export markets and forced costly relocations. (10) A GRADUATE MISMATCH — universities expanded new-energy programmes into a contracting labour market, so the education system amplified rather than absorbed the shock.
risiko_sosial_indonesia: (1) SINGLE-INDUSTRY REGIONAL COLLAPSE. Morowali (35 smelters, 22 in IMIP, ~86,000 Indonesian workers plus ~24,000 contractors) and Weda Bay (32 smelters, 19 in IWIP, 81,000+ workers) are already exposed: RKEF utilisation has fallen to ~76%, PT Gunbuster idled 18 of 22 furnaces in March 2025, and the 2026 ore quota was cut ~30%. Because these workers left farming and fishing, layoffs convert directly into poverty rather than into reabsorption by the traditional economy. Indonesia has no equivalent of a state-directed reemployment programme, and the regions have the thinnest safety nets in the country. (2) STRANDED EXPORT FACTORIES. Kendal and Batang were built for a US market now subject to 121-178% combined duties. Idle plants in SEZs mean lost jobs, wasted incentives and a political backlash against foreign investment. (3) FISCAL AND SOE EXPOSURE. If Danantara, IBC, Antam, PLN and Himbara banks underwrite battery and solar capacity that then runs at low utilisation, the losses land on the state balance sheet and ultimately on taxpayers — the Chinese pattern, without China's fiscal depth. (4) A 320 GWh MAINTENANCE CLIFF. Eighty thousand village systems with 4 MWh batteries each, owned by cooperatives with ~1% institutional readiness, is a recipe for mass premature failure within 5-8 years — dead batteries, dark villages, and a discredited technology. Indonesia's own history of failed village solar programmes (PLTS komunal from the 2010s, many non-functional within years) is the direct precedent. (5) ENVIRONMENTAL AND WASTE BURDEN. No module or battery recycling infrastructure, no extended producer responsibility, and HPAL tailings disposal questions in Halmahera — a hazardous-waste problem accumulating with no owner. (6) OCCUPATIONAL SAFETY. 93 recorded accidents over eight years to 2023 at IMIP, and 13 deaths plus 46 injuries in one December 2023 furnace fire, indicate a safety regime that will not withstand a rapid battery-manufacturing scale-up. (7) LABOUR AND SOCIAL FRICTION around large Chinese expatriate workforces (~16,000 at IMIP), which has already produced disputes and periodic unrest and is easily politicised. (8) LAND AND CONSENT CONFLICTS from utility-scale solar and from expanded mining, particularly where customary (adat) land is involved. (9) ELITE CAPTURE OF THE COOPERATIVE PROGRAMME — 80,000 KDMPs handling energy assets creates 80,000 procurement opportunities with weak audit capacity. (10) DEPENDENCY LOCK-IN — if Indonesia builds 100 GW entirely on imported Chinese cells, inverters and BESS with no domestic capability, it converts an energy-import dependency (fuel) into an equipment-and-spares dependency, with strategic exposure to a single supplier country.
unintended_consequences: (1) CHEAP CHINESE OVERCAPACITY IS SIMULTANEOUSLY INDONESIA'S BIGGEST GIFT AND ITS BIGGEST TRAP. Sub-RMB-1/W modules and US$50-60/kWh cells make Indonesian decarbonisation affordable a decade earlier than expected — while making Indonesian manufacturing of the same products permanently unviable. Policymakers cannot have both; pursuing manufacturing self-sufficiency will raise deployment costs and slow the transition. (2) THE BATTERY CHEMISTRY RUG-PULL. Indonesia banned nickel ore exports and built an entire industrial strategy on nickel demand from NCM batteries — and the market moved to LFP and now sodium-ion (US$50-56/kWh in 2026, approaching lithium parity). The downstreaming programme may be completed just as its core demand thesis dissolves. (3) US TRADE POLICY AS AN INVESTMENT DRIVER AND THEN A DESTROYER. American duties pushed Chinese capacity into Indonesia, and American duties are now closing it — Indonesia's solar manufacturing base was created and may be destroyed by the same foreign policy instrument, with no Indonesian agency in either direction. (4) SOLAR MAKING COAL MORE EXPENSIVE, NOT LESS. Because PLN holds take-or-pay coal PPAs and the Java-Bali grid is already oversupplied, adding solar raises system cost in the short run and gives PLN a genuine financial reason to resist the president's own programme — an internal contradiction that no amount of target-setting resolves. (5) ANTI-INVOLUTION EXPORTING THE PROBLEM. China's domestic capacity restraint (energy standards, consumption taxes from September 2026, capacity buyouts) increases the incentive to build offshore — so Chinese overcapacity discipline may accelerate, not slow, capacity accumulation in Indonesia. (6) THE RUSH-TO-INSTALL CLIFF. China's June 2025 pricing reform produced 212 GW in H1 2025 and a 66% collapse in H1 2026. Any Indonesian deadline-driven incentive (a TKDN deadline, a quota year-end, a COD cut-off) will produce the same boom-bust in miniature — and the June 2026 COD deadline attached to the import-relaxation window is exactly such a trigger. (7) GREEN JOBS PROVING CYCLICAL. 'Green job' rhetoric implies stability; the Chinese record shows new-energy manufacturing employment is as cyclical as commodities. Indonesian workforce planning built on permanent green employment will mis-forecast. (8) SUCCESS IN VILLAGE SOLAR UNDERMINING PLN'S BUSINESS MODEL, since the most expensive-to-serve customers are the first to leave the grid — the classic utility death-spiral, arriving in Indonesia from the periphery inward rather than from the affluent suburbs outward as in Australia and California. (9) THE COOPERATIVE MODEL CREATING 80,000 NEW PROCUREMENT ENTITIES with no track record, at a moment of maximum hardware availability and minimum oversight capacity. (10) INDONESIA'S NICKEL QUOTA CUTS WORKING TOO WELL — pushing LME nickel back to US$20,000/tonne by May 2026 revives idled capacity elsewhere and invites the next expansion cycle, exactly as China's 2016 coal supply-side reform did.
kelompok_rentan: (1) NICKEL SMELTER WORKERS AND THEIR FAMILIES in Morowali, Bahodopi, Konawe and Weda Bay — roughly 167,000+ direct Indonesian workers plus contractors, most of whom migrated from farming and fishing and have no fallback livelihood, earning around the Rp4 million (~US$244) regional minimum wage and heavily dependent on overtime that disappears first when furnaces idle. (2) CONTRACT AND OUTSOURCED WORKERS (~24,000 at IMIP alone) who have the weakest severance protection and are cut first. (3) COASTAL AND FISHING COMMUNITIES near the industrial parks, already bearing tailings, air and water impacts, who face environmental damage without the wage compensation once employment falls. (4) INDIGENOUS AND CUSTOMARY-LAND COMMUNITIES in Halmahera, Sulawesi and Kalimantan facing expanded mining for the battery chain and land acquisition for utility solar. (5) VILLAGE COMMUNITIES ENROLLED IN THE 80,000-UNIT COOPERATIVE PROGRAMME, who bear the consequences if assets fail — they will be blamed for mismanagement of systems they had no capacity to maintain and no role in specifying. (6) SMALL SOLAR INSTALLERS AND SMEs who invested in rooftop capability and were stranded by the abolition of net metering and by unpredictable quotas. (7) COAL-DEPENDENT REGIONAL ECONOMIES in East and South Kalimantan and South Sumatra, facing managed decline with no transition plan. (8) RETAIL INVESTORS on the IDX concentrated in nickel, coal and battery-linked counters. (9) VOCATIONAL AND UNIVERSITY GRADUATES who enrolled in metallurgy and mining programmes during the 2021-2023 boom and will graduate into the downturn — the direct Indonesian analogue of China's new-energy graduate glut. (10) SMALL DIESEL-GENSET SERVICE OPERATORS AND FUEL DISTRIBUTORS in eastern Indonesia, a large informal economy that solar-plus-BESS will displace with no transition support.
kasus_china: CASE A — POLYSILICON, THE ANATOMY OF A GLUT AND ITS STATE-MANAGED CLEANUP. Polysilicon fell from RMB 230,000/tonne to RMB 65,000/tonne during 2023 (-70%) and a further ~40% in 2024, taking prices below cash cost. By 2025 global output of ~1.9 million tonnes ran against capacity above 3.2 million tonnes — under 60% utilisation. The response was a three-part state intervention: draft mandatory energy-consumption standards issued for comment in September 2025 (effective January 2027) to legally close old lines; the December 2025 registration of Beijing Guanghe Qiancheng Technology, jointly owned by leading producers with an initial RMB 3 billion capital base and a proposed RMB 50 billion fund, to buy and scrap roughly one million of 3.5 million tonnes of capacity; and a 2% consumption tax on PV cells from 1 April 2027 rising to 4% in 2028. Notably, a parallel attempt to form an explicit output-quota JV was blocked by regulators on antitrust grounds. Daqo New Energy's shrinking revenues and narrowing losses through 2025 typify the survivors. CASE B — THE HUMAN LEDGER.
