Across 110 listed Chinese solar companies, headcount went from 776,750 (2023 peak) to 622,207 (end-2024): 154,543 jobs lost in one year, over 220,000 across two years, with LONGi, Tongwei, Trina, Jinko and JA Solar collectively shedding roughly 80,000-90,000 and cutting more than 30% of their workforces in 2024. Over 40 firms went bankrupt, were acquired or exited. CASE C — THE DEMAND CLIFF. China installed a record 315 GW in 2025, including 212.21 GW in H1 alone as developers rushed ahead of the 1 June 2025 shift to market-based renewable pricing. H1 2026 additions then collapsed 66% to 72.07 GW, and CPIA cut its full-year forecast to 180-240 GW — the first annual decline since 2019, dragging BNEF's global 2026 forecast to 649 GW versus 690 GW in 2025, the first global contraction on record. This is a textbook case of a policy deadline manufacturing a boom and then a bust. CASE D — BATTERIES, THE SAME MOVIE ONE REEL BEHIND. Planned national capacity approaching 5,000 GWh implies utilisation below 40%; power-battery capacity of ~4,800 GWh faces ~1,000 GWh of demand; stationary-storage cell output of ~557 GWh in 2025 was more than double global storage installations. LFP cells fell from ~US$110/kWh (early 2023) to US$50-60/kWh (late 2024), and sodium-ion reached US$50-56/kWh in 2026. Consolidation is brutal: only 33 firms had meaningful domestic vehicle-battery installations in January 2026 and 30 in February, with the top 10 taking 94.1% and CATL plus BYD alone at ~65%. In January 2026 four agencies summoned 16 leading firms to warn against below-cost pricing. CASE E — THE HISTORICAL RHYME. The 2011-2013 bust — polysilicon from US$500/kg (2008) to US$20-30/kg, module prices -40% in 2011, US anti-dumping duties in 2012, and the 2013 bankruptcies of Suntech (after missing a US$541 million bond payment) and LDK (which had been generating over 93% of Xinyu city's solar tax receipts) — established that this industry's cycle is structural, not accidental. China survived it only because domestic installation exploded from 2013 to 2015. That backstop is precisely what Indonesia lacks.
padanan_indonesia: The closest Indonesian analogue is NOT solar — it is NICKEL, and it is already at the bust stage. The parallel is nearly exact: state industrial policy (the 2020 ore export ban) plus abundant cheap capital plus Chinese technology and ownership (~65% of refining capacity, led by Tsingshan and Jiangsu Delong) produced an RKEF build-out across Sulawesi and Halmahera from 2021 to 2023 that overshot demand; prices then collapsed from over US$48,000/tonne (early 2022) to ~US$15,000/tonne (July 2025); LME inventories exceeded 250,000 tonnes; RKEF utilisation fell to ~76%; PT Gunbuster Nickel Industry delayed US$47 million in supplier payments and idled 18 of 22 furnaces in March 2025; Nickel Industries Ltd's EBITDA margin went from 34% (2022) to -7% (2024). The government's response is the Chinese playbook exactly: administrative supply control, cutting the 2026 RKAB ore quota to 250-270 million wet tonnes from ~379 million in 2025 (about -30%) and explicitly targeting a US$18,000-20,000/tonne price band — which pushed LME nickel back to US$20,000/tonne by 6 May 2026. This is Indonesia's own anti-involution, arrived at empirically rather than by learning from China. In SOLAR the equivalent is at the pre-bust stage: Trina Mas Agra Indonesia (Kendal, 1 GW to 3 GW), SEG Solar Batang (5 GW cell / 3 GW module plus 3 GW ingot-wafer from Q3 2026) and LONGi's ~1.4 GW Jakarta plant were built primarily for export, against domestic demand of only ~1-3 GW/year, and were hit within roughly two years by US preliminary duties of 35.17% anti-dumping and 121-178% combined — the same trade-wall mechanism that closed China's export markets in 2012. In BATTERIES the equivalent is at the build-out stage: HLI Green Power (Karawang, operating since July 2024, ~Rp13.5 trillion, ~10 GWh targeting 30 GWh) and the CATL-Antam-IBC project (US$5.9-6 billion, groundbreaking June 2025, 6.9 GWh scaling to 15 GWh, launch targeted 2026) — entering a global market where China alone already has ~4,800 GWh of planned power-battery capacity running at ~50-55% utilisation. In DEPLOYMENT Indonesia is pre-boom: 1.49 GW cumulative against a 100 GW target compressed to three years after the May 2026 blackouts, with the 80,000-village KDMP delivery vehicle at ~1% readiness.

catatan_kontradiksi_data: (1) INDONESIA'S SOLAR CAPACITY FIGURES CONFLICT ACROSS SOURCES. pv magazine reports 1.49 GW cumulative in early 2026, while Mordor Intelligence reports an Indonesian solar market of 2.15 GW in 2025 rising to 2.97 GW in 2026. These are almost certainly different measures (AC versus DC, grid-connected versus total including off-grid, and market-size versus installed-base), and market-research figures for Indonesia are frequently inflated. The IRENA/pv magazine figure is preferred here. (2) ROOFTOP SOLAR: ~479 MWac (~600 MWp) at end-2025 versus cumulative quota allocations of 1,905 MW for 2024-2025 — the gap reflects quota not being taken up, not a data error, but sources rarely make this explicit. (3) RENEWABLE MIX PERCENTAGES ARE INCONSISTENT: 14.65% (2024), 15.75% (2025) and 17.89% (April 2026) are quoted variously as primary-energy mix and as power-generation mix; the near-2-point jump in four months is implausible for a like-for-like measure and likely reflects a definitional or methodological change. Treat the trend, not the level, as reliable. (4) CHINA'S BATTERY OVERCAPACITY IS REPORTED AT WIDELY DIFFERENT SCALES: '>2 TWh capacity, 60% above demand' (2024), 'planned capacity approaching 5,000 GWh, utilisation below 40%', and 'power-battery planned ~4,800 GWh vs ~1,000 GWh demand, utilisation ~50-55%'. These differ on whether 'capacity' means built, commissioned or announced/planned, and whether storage cells are included. Announced capacity substantially overstates real capacity in every Chinese source. (5) CATL-ANTAM PROJECT VALUE AND TIMING VARY: US$5.9 billion versus US$6 billion, and initial capacity of 6.9 GWh versus 15 GWh, with launch dates given as 'end of July 2026', 'end of 2026' and 'by the end of the decade' for the 15 GWh expansion. Indonesian and Chinese press releases conflate phase-1 and full-project figures routinely. (6) HLI GREEN POWER CAPACITY is variously stated as 10 GWh and 'expanding to 30 GWh'; the 30 GWh figure is a stated ambition, not committed capacity. (7) IWIP EMPLOYMENT: '>81,000 Indonesian workers by early 2025' versus a '100,000 by early 2026' target — the latter is a target, frequently reported as if achieved. (8) NICKEL QUOTA FIGURES vary between 250 and 270 million wet tonnes for 2026 against ~379 million in 2025, and the implied cut is reported as anywhere from 30% to 35%. (9) US AD/CVD RATES for Indonesia are quoted as 35.17% (anti-dumping alone) and 121-178% (combined with countervailing duties, and varying by exporter); headlines frequently conflate these. Final determinations were due 13 July 2026 and may differ materially from the preliminaries. (10) CHINA SOLAR JOB LOSSES: '154,543 in 2024 across 110 listed companies' versus 'over 220,000 over two years' versus 'top-five firms cut over 30%' — these are overlapping, not additive, and none captures the much larger unlisted supply chain, so the true figure is likely understated. (11) TKDN: the nominal requirement is 60% from January 2025, ESDM proposed 40%, and an April 2025 reform exempts projects with over 50% foreign financing — sources disagree on what is actually in force at any given date, which is itself a finding about Indonesian regulatory instability.
